full_text:
Scott Fish Bowl is here! Year 16 is upon us, and we have reached video game levels of scoring! What makes SFB unique is the charity side of fantasy football, worldwide live drafts, and the incredibly complex scoring that Scott Fish himself comes up with each year. Luckily, we’ve got you covered with custom projections and player analysis built specifically for this year’s scoring.

Last year, in SFB15, the big focus was on volume kings with extra juice towards any players who may have a defensive impact as well. This season, Scott Fish has juiced scoring with big-play boosters across all positions.

After we cover the scoring and projections, I’ll give you my favorite and least favorite targets at each position. Let’s get after it!

__Scott Fish Bowl 16 (SFB16) Scoring__
--------------------------------------

__In SFB16, the motto is “video game scoring.” Here is the scoring breakdown:__

+   __6 points for all TDs__

+   2 points for 2pt conversions
+   1 point for every 25 yards passing (.04 per yard)
+   1 point for every 10 yards rushing/receiving (.1 per yard)
+   __.5 per first down (rushing/receiving)__
+   .5 per reception (half ppr)
+   __1 point extra per reception for TEs__
+   __1 point extra per first down for TEs (rushing/receiving)__

__Can’t Forget The Video Game Boosters!__

+   +10 points for 300+ passing games

+   +10 points for 400+ passing games
+   +10 points for 100+ rushing/receiving games
+   +10 points for 200+ rushing/receiving games
+   +10 points for 40+ yard passing plays
+   +10 points for 40+ yard rushes
+   +10 points for 20+ yard receptions

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/bb03d640ee4e0472b8acde499488ab9113e0260a/6f8b0cef165800bf702c65d0077867838646472f)

The starting lineup is completely flex-based, with up to 8 spots for RB/WR/TE plus 2 Superflex spots, QB/RB/WR/TE. By staying positionless again this year, the variety of team building and start/sit decisions will be up to your wildest imaginations.

Below are our top-50 overall projected players by SFB16 scoring. The “Bonus” column reflects the points each player is getting from the “video game” bonuses, while the “Total” column is their full projection with everything included.

\> Scroll down for separate graphics by position, and feel free to check out [this sheet](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/10UKgW4FhL_n00YZsb2k5O3-BBpu7NV3mif33GuF6Fq8/edit?usp=sharing) for the full player list.

__Scott Fish Bowl 16 (SFB16) Player Projections__
-------------------------------------------------

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/bb03d640ee4e0472b8acde499488ab9113e0260a/6bfdc970b5020d742a10fbea3b10894d9e20a7c0)

### QUARTERBACKS IN SFB16

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/bb03d640ee4e0472b8acde499488ab9113e0260a/514eb7b50c4bb4f2388731395dfaeecc12dec61b)

In recent years, hyper-mobile QBs saw huge boosts to their scoring thanks to points per carry.

This year, the scoring has been simplified. While mobile QBs are still juiced up thanks to the half point per first down, everything else is much more “standard.” All touchdowns are worth 6 points, while there’s a standard 1 point for every 25 passing yards.

The big twist: booster-type scoring for those big plays and games! Now, when a QB throws for 300+ yards in a game, you get a 10-point bonus. If they hit 400+ yards, you get the 10-point bonus twice. Hello pocket passers!

Let’s take a look at the 300+ passing threshold. In 2025, this threshold was crossed 61 times in 272 games, which is about 22.5% of the time. __This was also the fewest 300+ yard passing games in a season since 2008__. Pocket passers will hit the bonus much more often compared to hyper-mobile QBs hitting the 100+ yard rushing bonus. There were zero 100+ yard rushing performances from QBs in 2025! 2022 was the last time it happened more than twice.

While the 400+ passing game booster is enticing to try and chase after, the likelihood is very slim. In 2025, only 6 QBs had a game of 400+ yards, and none of them did it more than once. The list of names is about as random as it gets: Matthew Stafford, Bryce Young, Jacoby Brissett, Russell Wilson, Joe Flacco, and Justin Herbert. That’s just six times in 272 games. That is barely over 2% of the time, meaning this is not a booster worth chasing, but if it happens, consider yourself lucky!

At the end of the day, the QB scoring is too juiced to ignore. The position is one of two where we have the greatest discrepancies in projections vs ADP. Currently, 26 QBs make up the top 50 players in total points. Over 50%!! But yet, only 14 are currently being drafted in the top 50. This means we can attack the scarce positions early, scoop up 2-3 QBs in the early-middle rounds to lock in that high-scoring potential, and grab value at other positions later on!

​

*__BEST VALUE PICK:__* *Dak Prescott – Projects as a Top-6 overall player vs. ADP of 41*

*__WORST VALUE PICK:__* *Fernando Mendoza – Projects as QB31 (118 overall) vs. ADP of 86 – currently being drafted ahead of guys like Tyler Shough, and I can’t fathom why.*

### RUNNING BACKS IN SFB16

​![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/bb03d640ee4e0472b8acde499488ab9113e0260a/3c1a5f2a80e64d23e53d9f8ea36ef793dc882513)

Just like the QB position, the running backs return to a little bit of normalcy this year in SFB16. There are no more points per carry, BUT we still have half a point per first down, along with the half point per reception. Knowing that we still get rewarded for first downs, we want to continue focusing on the true bell-cow backs who get work in both the rushing and passing game.

Last year, 5 players had four 40-yard runs apiece: James Cook, Jonathan Taylor, De’Von Achane, Derrick Henry, and TreVeyon Henderson. Jahmyr Gibbs led the league with 6. In 2025, 41 total players recorded at least one rush of 40+. RBs can benefit from the receiving big play bonus, but they won’t do so nearly as often as WRs and TEs. For perspective, Christian McCaffrey and Chig Okonkwo had the same number of 20+ yard receptions last year.

While big plays make this format oh-so-fun, the real strategy is finding the consistency at the top of your draft. __The bonuses ensure those RBs who are__ *__both__* __primary ball carriers__ *__and__* __a top-3 target in their offense pop as absolute league winners in this SFB16 format. From a projection standpoint, the cliff is pretty steep.__

Currently, 7 RBs project to average 100+ rushing/receiving yards per game. For example, Christian McCaffrey hit this milestone in 12 of 17 games last year, guaranteeing you an extra 10 fantasy points per game 70.5% of the time, so prioritizing those top options early is important. If we fail to lock down a top 3 or 4 RB early on in drafts, do we bother drafting any? This is tricky, and we may have to debate this strategy in just a little bit.

​

*__BEST VALUE PICK:__* *Jonathan Taylor projected RB3 vs ADP 13 = RB4*

*__WORST VALUE PICK:__* *Bucky Irving projected 97th overall vs ADP 52*

### WIDE RECEIVERS IN SFB16

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/bb03d640ee4e0472b8acde499488ab9113e0260a/79d8450bac6357bf76aa252a172741b7505f8d23)

Now, we break down the most difficult position to grasp in SFB16. For most fantasy managers, WR is a priority position. While volume-based WRs are still important, we have to account for the big play guys who can see a 10-point fantasy spike off of one 20+ yard play, or even multiple. The big play wide receivers can outperform your “PPR cheat code” players, as 3 catches for 80 yards can result in more fantasy points than 7 catches for 80 yards, thanks to the big-play bonuses.

308 different players had at least one 20+ yard catch. 76 of them (~25%) had exactly one. Your elite-tier guys — Puka and JSN — hit the threshold 27 times. Dominant possession guys who also have big play upside are complete cheat codes in this video game format.

It’s important to remember that while big plays and volume are important, WRs still get the 10-point booster just as the RBs/TEs do for eclipsing the 100-yard scrimmage mark. While elite names keep repeating themselves like Puka/JSN, it’s important to remember elite perimeter receivers, such as AJ Brown (now in a new home), George Pickens, and Tee Higgins are boosted in this type of format.

Similar to the RB position, the WR’s are just as top-heavy. Players like Puka Nacua come in with a 30-point projection greater than the overall WR2. That is insane. But unlike the RBs, there is value to be found further down the board, and once we lock in our elite producer, it is a position that we can come back to after we hit RB/QB. There is a legit opportunity for you to start a draft with Jonathan Taylor, Justin Jefferson, and Dak Prescott, and you would have three top-20 projected players within your first three picks; thanks to Dak’s ADP being in the early 40s (late 3rd round).

*__​BEST VALUE PICK:__* *Justin Jefferson projects as 10th overall vs ADP 15*

*__WORST VALUE PICK:__* *Chris Olave projects as 54th overall vs ADP of 39*

### TIGHT ENDS IN SFB16

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/bb03d640ee4e0472b8acde499488ab9113e0260a/1a3b392f6e613159301fcc76e2564cfdec00f566)

This is my favorite group of players to scoop up value! Thanks to the TE position getting an extra point per reception over the RBs/WRs, high-volume TEs – who are usually a top-2 target on their team – get an advantage over high-touchdown rate ones.

TEs have the unique opportunity to turn a 10-yard catch for a first down into a 4-point play. With target hogs like Trey McBride, it is easy to envision how and why they project higher than in your traditional TE premium leagues. Some managers in your live drafts may recognize these bonuses, and you could see top guys like Bowers and McBride go early in the first round. __However, I will not be one of these people because there is still so much value down the board, and the cliff fall at RB/WR is steeper than at TE.__

While we don’t see TEs cross the century mark in scrimmage yards too frequently, we have seen an increase in TE usage across the league. Still, only 7 tight ends eclipsed the century mark last season, and McBride was the only one to do this more than once.

The real leverage play is leaning into the TE premium scoring. Find target machines who can capitalize on the extra point-per-reception + point-per-first-down, but also the big play guys with YAC ability who can play like a big body receiver, or are a top-2 target on their respective teams. Obvious names immediately jump out, such as Brock Bowers and Colston Loveland, but the list is deeper than you may expect.

Prioritize volume first, and then lean towards elite athleticism to break any draft ties. There is a sweet spot with the TEs based on projections. There are 12 TEs projected in the top 100 players, but then we hit a pocket of 14 TEs ranked between the 100th and 150th overall players.

The TE position is incredibly valuable for filling your various flex positions. Top-ranked TEs like Tyler Warren project for the same level of fantasy production as 2nd round picks James Cook and Saquon Barkley. The difference, though, is that Tyler Warren is drafted on average 20 picks later. Forgotten TEs like Hunter Henry project within a few points of Marvin Harrison Jr,, but have a 27-pick gap in ADP.

*__BEST VALUE PICK:__* *Travis Kelce projects 55 overall vs ADP of 103*

*__WORST VALUE PICK:__* *Harold Fannin projects 75 overall vs ADP of 55*

__OVERALL SCOTT FISH BOWL16 DRAFT STRATEGY__
--------------------------------------------

The ideal start to your Scott Fish Bowl 16 draft is to lock down an elite player at a scarce position where we see a 2 to 3-point-per-game drop-off. The elite RB should be considered the most scarce position. I am not looking for time shares or third-down specialists. We need offensive focal points in the run and pass game to move the needle. If your draft slot doesn’t give you access to a top-3 RB, I’d simply forego the position in favor of QB or WR.

The opposite should be said for the QB position. In a league that rewards massive pass plays and 300+ yard passing games, the elite pocket passers can be just as reliable, or even outpace those hyper-mobile QBs. Think about passers who love to push the ball downfield and are not afraid of taking shots deep. Matthew Stafford just won the MVP with this play style, and even mildly mobile QBs like Brock Purdy are continuously undervalued. ADP doesn’t reflect the QB projections, so I’m willing to pass on the position in Rounds 1-2 before drafting multiple in Rounds 3-5, where elite production can still be found. I will let others chase the mobile QBs and focus on the elite pocket passers.

As tempting as it is to go for the top TE talents like Brock Bowers, I will most likely be forced to wait and draft a variety of different possession guys. SFB16 doesn’t care about youth. All that matters are reliable target hogs who are go-to pieces on 3rd-downs to get the team a first down, or who can break deep down the seam for the big chunk play bonus potential. Because of the cliff after the top RBs and WRs, I want to anchor those positions first before chasing the TE position. I really love to attack that pocket of players in the 80-145 overall range and hit the TE position a couple of times there.

Remember that SFB16 is positionless. We have 8-flex spots plus 2 Superflex spots. There are no positional limits that keep you from going heavier in one position group than another (besides QB with the ability to start two max). Because of this positionless fantasy football format, you have complete flexibility in roster construction. Get as creative as possible and forget your previous fantasy draft experiences because SFB16 embraces the chaos.
